processing: Dried jujubes are boiled for a long time until the water turns sweet, or jujubes preserved by slow simmering for eight hours to a day are diluted in boiling water.
harvest_season: Made from dried fruit, or preserved fruit and syrup, all year; sun-dried fruit is preferred for preserving.
appearance_dry: Wrinkled, glossy dried fruit in deep red-brown.
appearance_liquor: Deep ruby-brown to rich dark maroon.
taste_profile: Naturally sweet and fruity with a dried-date richness, thicker and syrupy when made from preserved jujube.

brewing.notes: Boil dried fruit gently for a long time, topping up if needed, and add honey only if you must. Pine nuts are the usual garnish. Amounts are a starting point.

vintage_note: No vintages or seasons: dried jujubes and jujube syrup are sold year-round. Look for fruit that is still supple, and read syrup labels for added sugar.
description:
Jujube tea is a dark, sweet drink made by boiling dried jujubes, the small red fruit also sold as Chinese red dates. It belongs to both Korea and China: Koreans know it as daechu-cha and count it as a traditional tea, while Chinese-speaking drinkers call it hongzao cha.

There are two routes. One is simply a long boil of dried fruit. The other is preserving first: sun-dried jujubes simmer on low heat for eight hours to a day until the liquid turns syrupy, and that preserve is then let down with boiling water.

The colour is impressive, a deep ruby-brown to dark maroon, and the taste is all fruit and sweetness with no bitterness. Long, slow cooking is what makes it good; a quick steep gives a thin cup. Pine nuts on top are the classic finish.

Shops sell ready-made syrup, which is the easy way in. Traditional claims about nerves, anaemia and appetite come with it, but enjoy it first as a sweet drink rather than a treatment.
history: Chinese-language and English sources describe it as a Chinese tea, while Korean sources call it a traditional Korean one. Little is documented about when it first became a named tea. A Korean encyclopedia entry covers it as daechu-cha, and in China a pre-made syrup is sold in grocery stores.
